claims.text: The initial material is a solutionized, single-phase, BCC refractory high-entropy alloy, exemplified by an NbTiAlZr-based system.
A precipitation heat treatment at 1000–1150 °C under an inert atmosphere, followed by tailored cooling, is the proposed intervention.
The proposed heat treatment will retain nanoscale sigma-phase precipitates.
Precise control of temperature, holding time, and cooling rate will produce uniformly dispersed nanoscale sigma precipitates without coarsening.
The heat treatment forms uniformly distributed nanoscale sigma-phase precipitates within the BCC matrix.
The nanoscale sigma precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
The nanoscale sigma precipitates reduce grain-boundary sliding.
Obstructing dislocation motion and reducing grain-boundary sliding will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Obstructing dislocation motion and reducing grain-boundary sliding will limit creep.
The treated alloy is expected to have 15–25% higher yield strength than the single-phase baseline.
The treated alloy is expected to have greater creep resistance than the single-phase baseline during service above 1000 °C.
The relevant baseline is a conventionally processed refractory high-entropy alloy that remains single phase and lacks engineered precipitates.
The predicted performance enhancement is bounded to refractory high-entropy alloys treated under an inert atmosphere and used above 1000 °C.
Small deviations in holding time or cooling rate may cause precipitate coarsening.
Precipitate coarsening may cause embrittlement and eliminate the expected mechanical-property improvements.
Failure to achieve at least approximately 15% yield-strength improvement or enhanced creep resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
